setting.placeName: Legation of the United States, Peking,

div.head: Mr. Williams to Prince Kung

dateline.placeName: Legation of the United States, Peking,

div.p: Sir: I have the honor to acknowledge your highness’s despatch of the 25th instant, in which you inform me “that the governor of Fuhkien complains that, when in Amoy, an American named Pih-chau attacked a Chinese named Ho Chu-lau, on the 17th of last July, for interfering to prevent a row, and with twenty armed and drunken foreigners robbed his shop and carried off Ho Fah, one of his assistants, as their prisoner; and that when the sub-prefect informed Mr. Irwin, the American consul, of the case, he merely had Ho Fah set at liberty, but never examined or punished one of the foreigners who had caused the disturbance; and, lastly, that Mr. Irwin is an old man, ignorant of public business, one whom the foreigners do not at all fear or respect, so that by their excesses the trade of the port is much interfered with,” &c., &c.

On perusing this despatch it occurred to me that when Mr. Bradford was consul at Amoy the number of foreigners there who had no employment was small, while, since the recapture of Chang-chau from the rebels, a large number of such men have been skulking about in that region. It is not, therefore, because Mr. Irwin is now consul that they have no respect for the office and do not fear him. But why need the governor of Fuhkien, in speaking of the affairs of Amoy and that it was desirable that they should be conducted according to treaty stipulations, go out of his way to remark that “Consul Irwin is an old man, who is ignorant of public business?” Such remarks injure the good will and courtesy which should ever be maintained.

That foreigners should be going about wish arms, robbing in open day, and making prisoners of shopmen, as the despatch under reply mentions has been done in Amoy, showing that they have no fear of law, and yet none of them be arrested or punished, cannot be suffered. I will inquire into the particulars of the affair, and as soon as I learn the true facts respecting it I will further inform jour highness.
I have the honor to be, sir, your highness’s obedient Servant,
